definition: Generating text from structured graph input such as AMR or knowledge graphs, using encoders that operate over nodes and edges.
details: Generating text from structured graph input such as AMR or knowledge graphs, using encoders that operate over nodes and edges. It is a core architecture for data-to-text generation.

explainer.lead: Graph-to-sequence generation turns a structured network of entities and relationships into readable text. It matters because graphs can express information clearly, but people often need that information as a sentence, paragraph, or description.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a set of dots connected by labelled arrows, such as “dog” connected to “ball” by “chases.” Graph-to-sequence generation is like teaching a computer to look at that picture and write, “The dog chases the ball.” It reads both the dots and the connections before choosing the words.
tiers.practitioner: A graph encoder processes nodes and edges, and a text decoder generates the output sequence. This setup is applied to AMR-to-text and knowledge-graph-to-text tasks within data-to-text generation. A key pitfall is flattening the input in a way that loses edge or relationship information; generating fluent text also does not by itself establish that every relationship was preserved.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a graph G = (V, E), the task is to generate a token sequence y = (y1, ..., yT), commonly factorised as p(y | G) = product over t of p(yt | y<t, G). The encoder represents graph structure through computations over nodes and edges, while the decoder produces text. The formulation does not prescribe a particular encoder or decoder, and fluent generation alone does not guarantee faithful coverage of the input graph.

explainer.example: Take a graph with nodes “Maya,” “book,” and “write,” connected so that Maya is the writer and the book is what was written. A graph-to-sequence system can encode those nodes and relationships and generate the sentence “Maya wrote a book.”

usedIn.name: AMR-to-text generation
usedIn.detail: Produces natural-language text from an Abstract Meaning Representation graph.

usedIn.name: Knowledge-graph verbalisation
usedIn.detail: Expresses entities and their relationships as readable sentences or descriptions.

usedIn.name: Data-to-text generation
usedIn.detail: Uses graph-structured input as the basis for generating textual output.

explainer.intuition: A sentence puts words in a line, while a graph connects pieces of meaning in a network. Graph-to-sequence generation first understands that network, including its relationships, and then linearises the meaning into text.
howItWorks: Provide a structured graph whose nodes and edges represent the input information.
Encode the graph by computing representations that use both nodes and edges.
Pass the resulting graph representation to a text decoder.
Generate output tokens in sequence until the text is complete.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a way to communicate graph-structured knowledge through natural language. It is a core architecture for data-to-text generation, bridging structured representations and text people can read directly.
misconceptions: It is not simply printing node labels: the edges and their relationships must inform the generated text.
It is not one fixed neural network design: the concept allows different graph encoders and text decoders.
A fluent sentence is not necessarily a faithful one; important graph relationships can still be omitted or misrepresented.

diagram.caption: Graph structure is encoded into a representation that guides sequential text generation.
